title: Why Living Leaders Almost Never Appear on Money — Unless They're Royalty
hook: A count of nearly 1,000 world coins found sitting leaders appear almost exclusively in hereditary monarchies — which is why putting an elected president on currency reads as a monarchical move.
key_points: A survey of ~1,000 coins from 165 countries found only 13% feature the sitting head of state — 62% of monarchies do, versus under 1% of non-monarchies.
Of 340 new banknotes issued by 84 countries (2019–2024), about 15% depicted a sitting leader, again almost all monarchies.
Only two non-monarchies deviate: Samoa (parliamentary democracy) and Botswana (republic that traditionally features its sitting president).
The author's argument: featuring an elected, living leader on currency would be 'highly abnormal' for a republic and echoes monarchical practice.
content_html: A political scientist went looking for a simple fact: how many countries put their current, living head of state on their money? Jacques Hymans counted nearly 1,000 circulating coins from 165 countries and 340 new banknotes issued by 84 countries between 2019 and 2024. The pattern was stark — only 13% of countries feature their sitting leader on coins, and virtually all of them are hereditary monarchies (62% of monarchies do it, versus under 1% of republics and other non-monarchies).
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, Hymans found the same split on banknotes: about 15% of countries issued new bills depicting a sitting leader in that five-year window, again concentrated almost entirely in monarchies. Only two non-monarchies broke the pattern — Samoa, a parliamentary democracy, and Botswana, a republic that has long featured its sitting president. His conclusion is that the practice isn't a neutral design choice; it tracks regime type so closely that a republic adopting it would be aligning itself, visually, with monarchical rather than democratic tradition — which he ties to broader concerns raised by critics about "monarchical ambitions" in the context of U.S. proposals to feature President Trump on coins or bills. (This card describes a global comparative pattern; the U.S. proposal is one current example of it.)

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Jacques Hymans, Adjunct Associate Professor of Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences; University of Southern California

related.title: Monarchies, Republics & Regime Types
related.hook: Is the head of state a queen or a president? That old question — monarchy or republic — turns out to matter less than whether real power is elected and accountable.

related.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
related.hook: The deepest dividing line between regimes isn't left versus right — it's whether power can be lost. Can the people remove their rulers, or not?

flashcards.prompt: What did a count of nearly 1,000 world coins find about who appears on them?
flashcards.back_html: Only 13% feature the sitting head of state — and almost all of those are hereditary monarchies (62% of monarchies vs. under 1% of non-monarchies).

flashcards.prompt: Which two non-monarchies were found to be exceptions, featuring their sitting leader on currency?

choices.text: Every democratic republic does this routinely

flashcards.explanation_html: The study found almost every non-monarchy avoids depicting its sitting leader on currency; Samoa and Botswana were the rare exceptions.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the author call putting a living elected leader on currency 'highly abnormal' for a republic?

choices.text: Because the practice is concentrated almost entirely among hereditary monarchies, not republics
Because it is illegal under international law
Because currency never depicts any person, living or dead

flashcards.explanation_html: The pattern in the data ties the practice to monarchy specifically, so adopting it in a republic breaks from near-universal republican norms.
